payload.message:
I'm going to push back on this one rather than implement it as written, because the technical premise doesn't hold for the primitive types — and following it literally would measurably hurt the code we just built.

**The covariance premise is true only for reference types, not primitives.** Java array covariance means `String[]` *is an* `Object[]`, so a single `swap(Object[], i, j)` already handles every object/`T[]` case. But `int[]`, `long[]`, `double[]`, `float[]` are **not** `Object[]` — an `int[]` is a single `Object`, but it is not an array of `Object`. So they cannot be passed to an `Object[]` swap; it won't compile. That means an `Object[]` helper consolidates the *one* object swap with itself — it can't touch the four primitive ones.

**The only mechanism that truly unifies all five is `java.lang.reflect.Array.get/set`:**

```java
static void swap(Object array, int i, int j) {           // accepts int[], double[], T[]...
    Object tmp = Array.get(array, i);                    // boxes a primitive every call
    Array.set(array, i, Array.get(array, j));            // reflects + unboxes every call
    Array.set(array, j, tmp);
}
```

This compiles for everything — but `swap` is the **hottest path in the sort** (called O(n log n) times). Routing every swap through reflection + autoboxing would slow the primitive sorts by roughly an order of magnitude and reintroduce per-element boxing — which is the exact thing the primitive overloads exist to avoid. The same objection kills the "delegate to a common location" fallback: for distinct primitive types there's no shared location to delegate the actual `temp = a[i]; a[i] = a[j]; a[j] = temp` to without that boxing.

**So the four primitive `swap`s are irreducible.** Each is 4 lines, type-specific, and unavoidable in Java — this is exactly why `java.util.Arrays` also keeps separate per-type swaps rather than one generic helper. Consolidating them doesn't reduce real redundancy; it trades a trivial, fast, idiomatic duplication for a slow, reflective one. That's a net regression.

My recommendation: **leave the swaps as they are.** But it's a judgment call with a real tradeoff, so here are the honest options:

| Option | Effect | My take |
|--------|--------|---------|
| **Leave as-is** | 4 primitive + 1 generic swap, all fast | Recommended — the "duplication" is irreducible and zero-cost |
| **`Object[]` for object path only** | Drop `<T>` generic swap in favor of `swap(Object[],…)`; primitives unchanged | Purely cosmetic; still 5 methods. No real win |
| **Reflection-based single helper** | One `swap(Object,…)` for all 5 types | Not recommended — ~10× slower primitive sorts, reintroduces boxing |

If you want the single-helper version anyway — e.g. this is for a context where readability outweighs sort throughput — tell me and I'll implement the reflection one with the cost clearly documented. Otherwise I'll leave the swaps fast and type-specific. Which way do you want to go?
